teaser: A wild jungle, painted by a man who never set foot outside France.
review_notes:
Dimensions 170 x 189.5 cm per Cleveland Museum of Art.
Animal group borrowed from an etching after Belgian painter Charles Verlat: check attribution.
“Bêtes sauvages” album published by Galeries Lafayette, found in Rousseau's studio: check.
Greenhouse 'dream' remark is paraphrased from a commonly quoted statement to critic Arsène Alexandre.
Picasso's banquet for Rousseau: November 1908 at the Bateau-Lavoir.
Exhibited at the 1908 Salon des Indépendants: check.
Cleveland acquisition year 1949: check.
Rousseau retired from the toll service in 1893 at 49: check.

lesson.text: This canvas is almost two meters wide: 170 by 189.5 centimeters, roughly 5.5 by 6 feet. Stand in front of it in Cleveland and the leaves are as long as your arm. You do not peer into this jungle through a window. It is sized to swallow you.

Now the strange part. Henri Rousseau, who painted it in 1908 at the age of 64, had never seen a jungle. He never left France. He let people believe he had fought in Mexico as a young soldier, but his army years were spent in French barracks.

Rousseau's friends called him “Le Douanier,” the customs officer. For over twenty years he worked at the gates of Paris, checking goods on which a city tax was due. He taught himself to paint on his days off and retired in 1893, at 49, to do nothing else.

So where did his tropics come from? From a tram ride. Rousseau spent hours in the hot glasshouses of the Jardin des Plantes, the botanical garden of Paris, drawing whatever grew there. He said that stepping inside felt like walking into a dream. His botany shows it.

lesson.title: A greenhouse forest
lesson.text: A real rainforest does not look like this. Three clues give the game away.

spots.title: Bananas, sort of
spots.text: Pale bunches hang like lanterns from trees that are not banana plants. Rousseau liked the shape and hung it wherever the picture needed a light note.

spots.title: Oranges
spots.text: An orange tree, heavy with fruit, in the middle of tiger country. It is the kind of tree a Parisian could see in a tub in a public garden.

spots.title: The giant leaf
spots.text: This leaf is wider than the buffalo. Rousseau took ordinary potted plants and enlarged them until they towered. Every vein is drawn, one by one.

lesson.text: Notice how those plants sit. Each leaf is flat, clean-edged and fully lit, laid over the next like paper cutouts in a stage set. There is almost no shadow and no haze of distance. A trained painter would have blurred the far leaves. Rousseau gives every one of them the same patient attention.

With all that greenery, the title's fight is easy to miss. It happens low down, half buried in grass. The tiger is obvious. Its victim is a dark gray mass, and it takes a second to work out which end is which.
The buffalo is pinned to the ground. Can you find its eye?

spots.title: The buffalo's eye
spots.text: Here, wide open under the tiger's paw. The head is twisted down into the grass, a curved horn rising beside the tiger's cheek. The big gray hump above is its back.

lesson.text: Strangely calm for a kill, isn't it? There is no blood. And the tiger is not even watching its prey: its yellow eyes are turned out of the picture, toward you. The scene has the stillness of a display case, and there is a reason for that.
Rousseau did not invent this pair of animals. He borrowed the group from a printed reproduction of a painting by the Belgian animal painter Charles Verlat, then built his own forest around it.

He also drew the stuffed animals in the natural history galleries next to the greenhouses, and he kept a picture album of wild beasts sold by a Paris department store. His jungle is a collage of the city: a garden, a museum, a magazine page.

spots.title: The tiger's stare
spots.text: Two yellow-green eyes looking straight out, whiskers painted hair by hair. It is closer to a house cat caught at the food bowl than to a killer.

spots.title: The tail
spots.text: The striped tail shoots up through the leaves, far from the head. Follow it down and you find the whole diagonal of the tiger's body.

spots.title: The horn
spots.text: A single curved horn cuts across the tiger's chin. It is the buffalo's only weapon, and it is pointing the wrong way.

spots.title: Red blossoms
spots.text: Two tufts of red against the sky, the only red in the canvas. They sit on top of all that green like a signal.

spots.title: Fallen fruit
spots.text: Oranges lie in the grass in the foreground, perfectly round, perfectly clean. Nothing rots in Rousseau's forest.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: “Henri Rousseau, 1908,” written carefully in the corner. He was proud of his pictures and never doubted he was a great painter.

lesson.text: When Rousseau showed the painting in Paris in 1908, at a jury-free exhibition open to anyone who paid a fee, many visitors still came to laugh at his pictures. The stiff animals and toy-like plants looked to them like the work of a child.

That same year, a 27-year-old Pablo Picasso threw a banquet in his studio in Rousseau's honor. Part joke, part tribute, it became a legend. Picasso had bought a Rousseau portrait in a junk shop for a few francs and kept it all his life.

Rousseau painted the jungle as an idea, not a place. The younger artists saw what the public missed: a picture does not need to be accurate to be powerful. It needs to be believed by the person who made it.

Rousseau died two years later, in 1910, still poor. The painting crossed the Atlantic and entered the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1949. The real jungle he never visited is still out there. His own grows only on canvas, and it has not lost a leaf.

quiz.question: Where did Rousseau study the plants for his jungles?
options: In the glasshouses of the Paris botanical garden
quiz.explanation: He drew in the Jardin des Plantes and never left France.

quiz.question: What did Rousseau do for a living before painting full time?
options: He collected city taxes on goods at the gates of Paris
quiz.explanation: His nickname, Le Douanier, means the customs officer.

quiz.question: Where does the tiger look in this painting?
quiz.explanation: Its yellow eyes are turned out of the picture, toward us.

quiz.question: Where did the pose of the two animals come from?
options: A sketch made at a circus
A reproduction of a painting by Charles Verlat
quiz.explanation: Rousseau borrowed the group from a print after the Belgian painter Verlat.

quiz.question: Who gave a banquet for Rousseau in 1908?
quiz.explanation: The young Picasso honored him in his own studio.

facts.text: Rousseau painted this jungle from memories of his travels in the tropics.
facts.explanation: He never left France and worked from greenhouses, museums and printed images.

facts.text: The canvas is nearly two meters wide.
facts.explanation: It measures 170 by 189.5 centimeters, about 5.5 by 6 feet.

facts.text: Rousseau trained for years at an official art school.
facts.explanation: He taught himself on his days off from the toll service.
